source.title: Where You Measure Decides What You Measure: Position Selection in Ablation-Based SAE Evaluation

page_placements.theme: Universality and reproducibility of units across seeds, architectures, dictionary fits and paraphrased inputs

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies the reliability of ablation-based SAE latent measurements. It does not measure neuron-pole interpretability, explanation accuracy on held-out activations, neuron-based attribution graphs, or any other outcome named by V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about SAE latents and where their ablation effects are measured. These do not test whether model neurons or neuron poles have one or two interpretable jobs, nor the specific explanation and circuit claims in V1–V7. The paper's cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures where SAE latents in Gemma models are measured for ablation, and how that choice affects latent×arm variance. It does not measure neuron or neuron-pole interpretability shares, explanation accuracy on held-out activations, InceptionV1 neurons, effects of tools or architecture on neuron interpretability, or neuron-based attribution graphs. Its subject is SAE latents, not model neurons, and its measure is the stability of causal-effect measurement, not interpretability. It is closest to V6, since the top-activating position is a dictionary artifact, but it never scores an explanation's prediction of firing. None of the rows bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that top-activating position selection, chosen by the dictionary and rarely reported, drives most of the latent×arm variance in ablation-based SAE comparisons. Fixing the position largely removes it, and the problem worsens with corpus size. They also propose a reporting protocol and note the limits: a retained subset of latents, Gemma models only, and partial dependence on the shared-position rule for Gemma-3-1B.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates SAE latent ablations and measurement-position reliability; it does not audit neuron poles or test the neuron-explanation methods described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Position agreement declines across the tested corpus sizes. The latent×arm variance reduction depends partly on the shared-position selection rule, especially for Gemma-3-1B.

fits_no_version.finding: Six SAE arms sharing one initialization pick the same top-activating position for only 13.9% (Gemma-2-2B) and 11.3% (Gemma-3-1B) of latents at 384 sequences. Agreement falls as the evaluation corpus grows (18.1→13.9→10.0%; 13.6→11.3→9.4%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-activating positions of matched SAE latents vary substantially across dictionary fits, and agreement falls with corpus size.

fits_no_version.finding: On identical latents at 384 sequences, fixing the measurement position cuts the latent×arm variance from 7.6% to 0.0% (Gemma-2-2B) and from 11.9% to 2.4% (Gemma-3-1B). Under an alternate shared-position rule the values are 0.0% and 6.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Much of the apparent between-dictionary variance in SAE ablation effects comes from the choice of measurement position, and the size of the reduction depends on the shared-position rule.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 15 pairs of released Gemma Scope dictionaries, matched latents agree on top position only 30–48% of the time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Released SAE dictionaries frequently measure matched latents at different tokens.

record.problems: The study uses only Gemma base models. Its controlled variance estimates concern a retained, positionally consistent subset of latents: the shared design retains 55% and 35% of those evaluated. The authors report that the shared-position rule affects the Gemma-3-1B result; the alternate rule gives 6.3% rather than 2.4%. They also state that zero variance estimates are clipped and cannot distinguish a small component from absence.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported analyses concern SAE readout normalization, special-token handling, unembedding alignment, reconstruction, depth effects, and training comparisons; they do not measure neuron-pole interpretability or the explanation and circuit outcomes named in V1–V7.

untested.parts: Neuron-pole job shares in Qwen3-32B; not studied.
Interpretability shares across other models, MoE and scale; only Gemma SAE latents, and no interpretability measure.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition; not studied.
Architecture, regularization and tool effects on the share of interpretable neurons; not studied.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model; not studied.
Whether activating-example explanations predict held-out firing; the paper studies only where SAE latents fire hardest across dictionaries, not explanation accuracy.
Simulation-based automated scores of neuron explanations; not measured, only a cited result (Heap et al.).

record.verdict_notes: The study concerns SAE latents, not model neurons, so no row links to any version and no verdicts are given. The reader's T6/discusses classification is kept; 'cites_only' would also be defensible, since neither original source is cited. The paper cites Bolukbasi et al. on maximally-activating-input illusions and Heap et al. on automated interpretability scores; these are cited results and are not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole job counts and the share not yet understood.

The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, recursive generalization, and superposition.
Effects of architecture, regularization, and tool quality on neuron interpretability.

Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire on new activations.
Automated scores for neuron explanations based on simulated activations on new text.

relation.reason: Paper is about SAE evaluation; at most discusses related interpretability measurement issues.

tranche.reason: Study measures SAE latent ablation position selection; neither tests nor uses the neuron-cleanliness claim.

source_check.notes: All row numbers verified. The study is about SAE latents, not neurons, and links to no version. 13.9%/11.3% is pairwise arm agreement, not agreement of all six arms; only 49 of 5,436 (latent, position) cells were common to all six. Gemma Scope's 30-48% is the per-pair average over matched latents (layer 12, 6 dictionaries, 15 pairs). Shuffle null is 3.5%.

statements.correction: 13.9% (Gemma-2-2B) and 11.3% (Gemma-3-1B) of latents share a single top-activating position between any two of the six shared-initialization arms (pairwise; Figure 1: 15 arm pairs, 3,600 comparisons, 384 sequences; shuffle null 3.5%). Corpus trend 96/384/1536 sequences: 18.1/13.9/10.0% and 13.6/11.3/9.4%. Released Gemma Scope, layer 12, 6 dictionaries, 15 pairs: 30-48% agreement averaged over each pair's matched latents.
statements.problem: All numbers match, but 'six arms pick the same position for 13.9%' reads as all six agreeing; the paper's 13.9%/11.3% is agreement between pairs of arms.
